stateSpace.title: Experiment 1: Explore the states allowed by flags
stateSpace.description: Toggle the fields and find combinations that satisfy the type but violate this screen's requirements.
stateSpace.rule: This screen hides previous results while refetching. It uses only four states: idle, loading, success, and failure.
stateSpace.invalid: The type permits this, but this screen's requirements do not.

reasons.loading-with-result: Data or an error remains while the request is loading.
reasons.two-results: Success data and a failure error are both present.

stateSpace.legend: Digits mean loading / data present / error present. 1 means present or true; 0 means absent or false. Payload contents are fixed: only presence combinations are counted.

exhaustiveness.title: Experiment 2: Where does adding a state cause a type error?
exhaustiveness.description: Select the four examples in order and compare State with the label function.

results.base: Type check passes: after handling all four states, state has type never.
results.extended: TS2345: cancelled is unhandled. That value cannot be passed to assertNever, which requires never.
results.fixed: Type check passes: cancelled is handled, leaving no unhandled type at the end.
results.fallback: Type check passes, but cancelled also returns Ready. This function no longer detects the missing case.

exhaustiveness.disclaimer: Repository tests check these displayed examples with the actual TypeScript compiler. This is not an editor that compiles code inside your browser.

boundary.title: Experiment 3: Separate input validation from state transitions
boundary.description: Validate JSON to load an order, then try recording a refund before payment or recording payment twice.
boundary.presetsLabel: Choose an input (selection alone does not change the order)
boundary.reloadNote: Successful validation replaces the current order with a new draft. This restarts the experiment; it is not a business state transition.
boundary.amountNote: amountYen is the order total. Recording a full refund does not change this value.
boundary.ready: The input has not been loaded yet. You can operate on the current order.
boundary.loaded: Validation passed. A new draft has been loaded.
boundary.rejected: Input rejected. The current order has not changed.
boundary.transitionRejected: This operation is not allowed in the current state. The order has not changed:

errors.not-draft: This entry point accepts only kind: draft.
errors.invalid-order-id: orderId must be a string containing more than whitespace.
errors.invalid-amount: amountYen must be a positive safe integer. Strings are not converted automatically.

boundary.disclaimer: This experiment runs entirely in your browser. It makes no network calls or payments. Record IDs are fixed samples; verifying real payments and controlling concurrent updates are out of scope.

extension.title: Experiment 4: Adding a state versus adding an operation
extension.description: The same requirement affects different locations depending on whether code is organized by state or by operation.
extension.caption: Each cell represents a design decision: how this operation behaves for this state.

union.case: Extend the union and update label and toDto. Exhaustiveness checks using never identify functions that need updating.
union.operation: Add an audit function that handles the three existing states. Usually, state definitions and existing functions do not change.

classes.case: Implement label and toDto in a Cancelled class. Callers using only the shared contract can stay unchanged, though construction and registration may still need updates.
classes.operation: Add audit to the shared contract and implement it in each class. Organizing operations in external functions or a Visitor changes this trade-off.

extension.caveat: This compares representative code organizations, not measured editing cost or performance. Shared implementations, Visitors, and sealed hierarchies provide additional design choices.
